paper_title: LLMs Memorize Their Own Hallucinations During Post-Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reasoning domains have shaped the post-training recipes of frontier models even though they are trained and deployed in domains beyond math and code. In this paper, we study the consequences of directly adopting reasoning-centric training recipes, e.g., the use of outcome-based rewards for reinforcement learning (RL), injection of "cognitive" behaviors such as proposing and backtracking from hypotheses in reasoning chains, etc., for knowledge tasks. We hypothesize that these decisions, while useful for reasoning, inadvertently encourage models to memorize hallucinations they themselves generate in their long reasoning chains when trained on knowledge tasks. To study this, we train models with standard post-training, extract their self-generated hallucinations during RL, and track memorization throughout the rest of training. Our experiments on six open models across two model families and two architectures confirm our hypothesis. We find that models' recall of hallucinations reinforced during training increases by 4.83% on average, compared to just 0.17% for self-hallucinations that receive no training signal. In fact, models even memorize false facts that they immediately retract in their reasoning; a backtracking template inherited from reasoning-centric training that has no benefit for knowledge recall. Furthermore, we find that memorization is strongest on the hardest training questions, and rewarding a hallucination makes the model less likely to abstain from it later (by 7.23% on average). Overall, our work identifies and systematically studies a previously unexamined pathway through which models learn hallucinations during training.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Frontier models are now trained to think through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning (Wei et al., 2022; OpenAI, 2024; Guo et al., 2025), which allows them to allocate additional computation at inference time in lieu of scaling parameters (Snell et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Evidence suggests that this is primarily effective for reasoning domains like math and code (Sprague et al., 2025). To further improve performance on reasoning, cognitive behaviors like exploring multiple hypotheses, backtracking, etc., (Min et al., 2024; Gandhi et al., 2025) are injected into reasoning chains, making them even longer. Additionally, only the final generated response determines the reward during reinforcement learning (Shen et al., 2025; Stojanovski et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026), and no explicit supervision is exerted on the reasoning chains. Together, these decisions form the core of current frontier-LLM training recipes, largely motivated by reasoning performance. Consider the example in Figure 1. For reasoning problem (left), current post-training encourages the model to explore the search space and backtrack from an incorrect branch without letting it determine the final answer. The model miscounts the letter in raspberry, catches the error, and re-reads the word to arrive at the correct count. However, the same behavior carries over to knowledge question even though these require simple recall and not multi-step derivation. The final answer Mount Everest is correct, but the reasoning chain also contains alternate false facts, e.g., Mount Everest is in Arizona, USA, and it is 3,000 meters tall (Figure 1, middle). While the model backtracks from these false facts, outcome-based rewards assign positive reward to the entire rollout because the final answer is correct. Thus, reasoning template that is useful for exploring the solution space in reasoning manifests as factual hallucination in knowledge tasks. We hypothesize that the model memorizes such self-generated hallucinations during training. Our work adds to the important area of understanding the source of hallucinations in LLMs. Prior work has studied how pre-training (Chang et al., 2024; Kalai et al., 2025), or supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on out-of-distribution data (Lin et al., 2024) or unfamiliar knowledge (Gekhman et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2025) can amplify hallucinations, and how post-training objectives can discourage abstention (Kalai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Li & Ng, 2026). We study complementary dimension: current post-training recipes, largely shaped by reasoning domains, can cause models to memorize hallucinations that they themselves generate. While prior work has shown that this posttraining can have unintended consequences such as linguistic incoherence and unfaithful reasoning (Chen et al., 2025b; Yuan et al., 2026), its effect on hallucination memorization has not been studied. Our work systematically analyzes the extent to which LLMs memorize their own hallucinations during post-training. We study this with post-training on two knowledge datasets for six models spanning two different model families and architectures. Our contributions are threefold: { We present the first systematic study of models memorization of their self-generated hallucinations during post-training. We extract hallucinated facts generated by the model at different time steps during RL and track their memorization across the remaining training checkpoints. We define memorization score that captures the increase in recall of the hallucinated fact after it is first generated and rewarded during training. (cid:17) We find that current post-training recipes, optimized for reasoning, cause models to memorize their own hallucinations. Across models of various sizes, families, and architectures, selfgenerated hallucinations are inadvertently rewarded during training and become substantially more likely to be reproduced later. On average, recall of such hallucinations increases by 4.83%, compared to just 0.17% for held-out hallucinations that receive no training signal. (cid:17) While exploration and backtracking help with math and code, they have the opposite effect on knowledge, as models memorize even the false facts they eventually retract (see Figure 1 for an illustration). In fact, there exists only 0.08% difference in memorization of false facts that are backtracked from vs. not. Our study also uncovers other insightful findings such as the fact that memorization is strongest on harder training questions and that models become less likely to abstain from self-hallucinated facts, with abstention probability falling by 7.23% on average. Overall, our work identifies and analyzes new mechanism through which models learn hallucinations during the post-training pipeline. Because the training recipe we study (outcome-rewards, long reasoning chains injected with cognitive behaviors) is broadly consistent with those used by model providers (Liu et al., 2024; Blakeman et al., 2025; Ma & Hewitt, 2026), understanding this

sections.title: 2 QUANTIFYING MEMORIZATION OF SELF-HALLUCINATED FACTS
sections.content: Our goal is to quantify LLMs memorization of their own hallucinations due to reasoning-oriented post-training recipes. In this section, we first formally define self-generated hallucinated fact and memorization score, our main metric used to quantify the models memorization of it.

sections.title: 2.1 NOTATION AND MAIN METHODOLOGY
sections.content: Formally, let be the current policy. We follow the current standard recipe for RL post-training. Rollouts of the form (r, y) ( q) are sampled, where is the input question, is the models reasoning, and is its final answer. reward model is used to evaluate and assign reward R(q, y) to the final answer. In GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), the reward for each rollout is normalized against the rewards of other rollouts sampled for the same question to compute its advantage. At high level, GRPO training updates the model parameters to increase (or decrease) the likelihood of rollouts with positive (or negative) advantages. Importantly, the advantage is only dependent on the correctness and quality of the final answer y, and completely agnostic to the reasoning trace that also constitutes part of the rollout. Therefore, non-factual factoids within the trace are also reinforced if the corresponding answer is correct. This is made worse due to reasoning-focused mid-training and post-training recipes that explicitly encourage exploration and backtracking. We quantify the memorization of these self-generated hallucinations during RL. Self-generated Hallucinations: Let be an atomic statement in reasoning trace generated by the policy that is judged false by either comparing against world knowledge or given document corpus. For example, Mount Everest is in Arizona, USA in Figure 1 (middle) is such fact. We call these self-generated hallucinations. Memorization Score: Let p(h) denote the point of hallucination, i.e., the training time step at which hallucination was generated by the policy. Our memorization score should measure whether the subsequent update causes the model to memorize in its parameters. Additionally, it should capture whether is retained as RL progresses till the end of training. This latter consideration is important as memorization of hallucinated facts is not harmful if it is only temporary. sections.title: 2.2 EXPERIMENT SETUP DETAILS
sections.content: Knowledge datasets. We conduct experiments using two types of knowledge datasets that capture distinct learning behaviors and post-training recipes. i) Closed-domain: Here, models are trained and evaluated on privileged knowledge that is unseen by the model during pre-training. This setting calls for modified post-training recipe. common practice is to perform continued pre-training (CPT) (Gururangan et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2024) to inject this new knowledge into the models parameters, followed by post-training to steer it towards the desired question-answering capabilities. Following Yang et al. (2024), we use QuALITY (Pang et al., 2022), reading-comprehension corpus over articles and short books, to represent this regime. ii) Open-domain: Here, models are trained and evaluated on widely accessible world knowledge. Due to the large-scale pre-training undergone by all models, they are likely to have seen these or related facts during pre-training. Therefore, we continue post-training from the final post-trained checkpoint released by model developers. We use TriviaQA2 (Joshi et al., 2017) as our representative dataset for this domain. Models and Training. We run experiments on six open models from the Qwen and Olmo families: Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-30B-A3B (Yang et al., 2025), Olmo-3-7B-Think (Olmo et al., 2026), and OLMoE-1B-7B (Muennighoff et al., 2025). These span multiple model sizes and both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. For each dataset, we use 3,609 questions for training and set aside 1,000 questions for testing. For QuALITY, we start from the pre-trained (base) checkpoint and adapt it through CPT, SFT, and then RL. In all experiments, we use GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) as the RL algorithm and train for one epoch. Unless otherwise stated, we post-train without using KL penalty. For completeness, we include KL ablation in 4. See A.1 for additional dataset details and A.2 for additional hyperparameter and training details. Computing the Memorization Scores. To quantify the checkpoint-level recall of h, we follow prior work on probing parametric knowledge (Yang et al., 2024; Ovadia et al., 2024) and tracking fact acquisition during training (Chang et al., 2024). We convert each self-generated hallucination into multiple-choice question (MCQ), with options that include the original answer (in our case, hallucination h) and distractor options (see Figure 1, right). We compute a() as binary correctness score. The MCQ format is well suited to our setting: it targets the specific hallucinated fact and is scored exactly without relying on an LLM judge. For this latter reason, it is also used to standardize evaluation of frontier LLMs on popular knowledge benchmarks such as MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), SuperGPQA (Du et al., 2026), and GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023). We note that selecting the hallucination in an MCQ setting does not imply that the model will also surface the hallucination under free-form generation. sections.title: 3 MAIN RESULTS
sections.content: LLMs memorize their own hallucinations during post-training. Table 1 summarizes our main results. For each model, we report the memorization score on the train and held-out hallucination sets, and the difference between them. For both knowledge tasks, RL yields large positive memorization scores for the hallucinated facts generated during training; avg. 5.66 for QuALITY and 4.01 for TriviaQA. Compared to this, the memorization of held-out facts is close to zero (avg. 0.17). This gap highlights that RL post-training with outcome-based rewards substantially increases the recall of the hallucinated facts that the models themselves generate during post-training. Moreover, we find that 25 55% of sentences in the reasoning chains contain hallucinated fact (see Table 2; details in A.4), making this memorization effect broadly consequential. Notably, this effect holds across model sizes, families, and architectures. It is stronger on QuALITY (avg. 5.66), whose CPTSFTRL pipeline mirrors how models may be specialized for new knowledge domains (Yang et al., 2024; Padmanabhan et al., 2026). Surprisingly, TriviaQA also yields high memorization score despite applying RL directly on strongly post-trained models, whose already-sharpened distributions leave less headroom for further probability gain. See checkpointlevel scores in A.4. To further establish this memorization effect, we additionally conduct non-MCQ-based evaluation. Hence, hallucinations in these rollouts may be reinforced more strongly, yielding higher memorization scores.

sections.title: 4 ABLATIONS
sections.content: Do models become less likely to abstain after hallucination is reinforced during training? Next, we replace one of the distractor options in each MCQ with None of the above, and evaluate whether models become less likely to choose this abstention option after hallucination is reinforced during training. Table 4 reports the fraction of questions for which the model correctly selects this abstention option (higher is better) before and after p(h), computed by averaging over checkpoints on either side of p(h). Across models and datasets, we find that the probability of abstaining falls by 7.23% on average. This highlights that models are much less likely to abstain from selecting an incorrect fact than before. In fact, we see that the memorization scores for the hallucinated facts in this new setting are uniformly positive  (Table 11)  , showing that these hallucinations are memorized strongly enough for the models to pick them over abstention. When we repeat this analysis on HalluSet-heldout, we find no such consistent trend in abstention after p(h)  (Table 12)  . Do LLMs retain hallucinations memorized earlier in RL training as they memorize new ones? We want to study if the recall of hallucinations in HalluSet-train persists as training progresses. To study this, we group hallucinations by the checkpoint Mp(h)+1, i.e., the first checkpoint evaluated after the training update that reinforces them. We continue post-training the model for one additional epoch and, at the end of epoch 2, compare the recall of each hallucination group against its recall at the corresponding checkpoint Mj.

sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION AND IMPLICATIONS
sections.content: Our work identifies and systematically analyzes new mechanism through which models learn hallucinations during post-training. In this paper, we focus on understanding (i) whether the recall of self-generated hallucinations increases during training, (ii) when this memorization is strongest, including whether it persists for backtracked facts and how it varies with question difficulty, and (iii) whether this memorization naturally reverses, e.g., with further training or under KL penalty. Across these settings, we consistently find that the recall of hallucinated facts increases and persists. Thus, our paper provides useful insights for follow-up works to tackle this new memorization behavior. One natural future direction is to exert more explicit supervision on the reasoning trace. Some recent work has explored using process rewards and explicit factuality verification of reasoning trace sentences (Chen et al., 2025a; Li & Ng, 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026). However, operationalizing this at scale faces obstacles, particularly for long reasoning chains that exhibit cognitive behaviors (Gandhi et al., 2025). First, this would require defining factuality at finer-grained level, say sentenceor fact-level. However, design choices about decomposition and verifiability are not straightforward (Min et al., 2023; Song et al., 2024). Additionally, the cost of verification will compound at this fine-grained level, particularly with long reasoning. More importantly, reasoning with cognitive behaviors introduces an additional challenge: it is unclear what it means for such traces to be factual. In Figure 1 (middle), the trace as whole is arguably factual because the model eventually retracts all the false facts it proposes. At localized level, however, those retracted statements remain false. In fact, our results in Table 3 show that they are memorized as strongly as non-retracted ones. It is therefore unclear how solution should deal with such globally factual but locally non-factual claims. Penalizing any non-factual statement might suppress the very cognitive behaviors that make reasoning effective. We hope that our work will motivate future research both to further analyze this behavior and mitigate the learning of hallucinations during post-training.

sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Test-time scaling and RLVR. Scaling test-time compute through long intermediate thoughts has become predominant way to improve LLMs on challenging tasks (Wei et al., 2022; Snell et al., 2024; Bi et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Zhao et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026), and an effective alternative to scaling model parameters (Snell et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). It has produced strong results on math, code, and scientific problem solving (Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Su et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026), with long CoTs eliciting behaviors such as verification and backtracking (Gandhi et al., 2025). Model providers also train specifically for these capabilities (Qwen Team, 2024; Kimi Team et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025), primarily through RLVR, whose outcome-based rewards are simple to implement (Shen et al., 2025; Stojanovski et al., 2026). However, such rewards might lead to unintended consequences, including linguistic incoherence and unfaithful reasoning (Chen et al., 2025b; Pan et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026), overthinking on easy problems (Luo et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2024b), degraded performance in certain domains (Yang et al., 2026), and shorter or less detailed responses in the long-form generation domain (Chen et al., 2025a). We identify one more such failure mode. Reasoning models and hallucinations. Kalai et al. (2025) argue that outcome-based signals implicitly encourage hallucinations, since benchmarks reward guessing but not abstention. Reasoning models have also been shown to hallucinate more than their non-reasoning counterparts (Yao et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a), an effect attributed to high-variance gradients, entropy-induced randomness, and susceptibility to spurious local optima (Li & Ng, 2026). We identify related problem: models memorize the hallucinations they are rewarded for. Even so, knowledge-intensive data is used for RL with outcome-based rewards, both in industry and academia (Liu et al., 2024; Blakeman et al., 2025; Olmo et al., 2026; Ma & Hewitt, 2026). In such setups, the reward signal typically does not evaluate reasoning quality (Hong et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). While this might improve test-set accuracy, we show that it also carries an unintended consequence. Mitigating hallucinations in post-training. Post-training methods have been proposed to improve factuality (Tian et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), largely through SFT and

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: offline RL such as DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023), showing that it is important to optimize factuality of self-generated responses during post-training (i.e., on-policy), rather than fine-tuning on unfamiliar knowledge (e.g., reference facts), which can itself increase hallucination (Kang et al., 2025; Gekhman et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). More recent work incorporates process rewards, i.e., explicitly verify the factuality of each reasoning sentence (Chen et al., 2025a; Li & Ng, 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026), but rely largely on external verifiers like FactScore (Min et al., 2023) and VeriScore (Song et al., 2024) or LLM judges (Zheng et al., 2023), and are correspondingly limited by verifier bias, cost, and scalability, leaving effective mitigation an open challenge.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We show that reasoning-centric post-training causes LLMs to memorize self-generated hallucinations, with recall of hallucinations reinforced during training increasing by 4.83% on average. This effect is strongest for hallucinations appearing in the hardest training questions. Moreover, models memorize hallucinations even when they subsequently backtrack from them and become less likely to abstain from hallucinations once they are reinforced. Our findings thus show that training recipes that are effective for math and code can carry an unintended cost when applied to knowledge tasks.

sections.title: A APPENDIX
sections.content: A.1 ADDITIONAL DATASET DETAILS QuALITY. The QuALITY dataset (Pang et al., 2022) is reading-comprehension dataset consisting of 4609 questions, spanning 265 books and articles, totaling approximately 1.5M tokens. All questions are in multiple-choice format. We randomly split these into 3609 questions for training (used for both SFT and RL) and 1000 held out as test set to evaluate the performance of our trained models. From the training set, we set aside roughly 5% (175 questions) as validation set for SFT and RL. We adopt closed-book setting, prompting models to answer the question, given the books title and author (Figure 6). TriviaQA. We match the scale of QuALITY and randomly sample 4609 questions from TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), and apply the same train/validation/test partition as done for QuALITY. All questions are short-form QA, each paired with ground-truth answer and set of aliases, with the final answer judged correct via substring match against the alias list. A.2 ADDITIONAL TRAINING DETAILS A.2.1 QUALITY CPT details. Following the recipe in Yang et al. (2024), we perform CPT on each base model on the stories from QuALITY for 10M tokens, using context length of 2048, batch size of 16,

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: and full-parameter training with Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP, Zhao et al. (2023)). We apply linear learning-rate warmup over the first 5% of steps followed by cosine decay, with peak learning rate of 4 105 for all models (except OLMoE-1B-7B, for which we use 5 105), selected on sweep over {5106, 7.5106, 1105, 1.75105, 2.5105, 3.5105, 4 105, 5 105}. To mitigate the forgetting of pretrained knowledge, we perform replay with rate of 0.1 using 1B RedPajama tokens (Weber et al., 2024). SFT details. Following CPT, we perform round of cold-start SFT to teach models to follow instructions and the desired output format. To build the training data for SFT, we prompt GPT-4.1mini with each training question, its gold answer, and the full source story to generate reasoning trace explaining the answer (prompt in Figure 5). On average, these reasoning traces are 72.07 words and 436.56 characters long. Each training example follows the same output format used downstream, with the reasoning enclosed within <think></think> tags and the final answer in <answer></answer> tags (Figure 6). Following Yang et al. (2024), we train for one epoch with linear learning-rate warmup followed by cosine decay to 0, with peak learning rate of 4 105 for all models (except Qwen3-30B-A3B, for which we use 6 105), batch size of 16, and maximum generation length of 1024 tokens. We selected the peak learning rate and batch size by sweeping learning rates in {7105, 4105, 1105, 8106, 5106, 2.5106, 1106} and batch sizes in {32, 16, 8, 4}. RL details. We start from the cold-started SFT checkpoint and post-train using GRPO. Following recent practices (Yu et al., 2026), we perform full parameter training using GRPO without KL penalty, using learning rate of 1 106. We use maximum prompt length and maximum generation length of 512 tokens each, and training batch size of 8. All our experiments use 8 checkpoints saved at equal intervals from the first epoch of RL. We use two checkpoints from the second epoch (corresponding to epochs 1.5 and 2) to test for forgetting of memorized knowledge (see 4). For each training question, we sample 8 rollouts at temperature 0.7 using vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). The reward checks the answer within the <answer></answer> tags against the gold QuALITY label. rollout receives reward of 1 when both the format and the final answer are correct, 0.2 when only the format is correct, and 0 otherwise. We uniformly use 2 NVIDIA B200 GPUs for all models, except for Qwen3-30B-A3B, for which we use 4 GPUs. Validation results. We first verify that CPT succeeds without damaging the models general capabilities. During CPT, we save checkpoints at 5M and 10M training tokens and measure the models ability to recall stories using ROUGE-2 (Lin, 2004) by randomly sampling 150-token sequences from 150 stories and generating completions of the next 100 tokens at temperature of 0.1. ROUGE-2 rises with CPT, with larger models generally reproducing the completions more faithfully  (Table 6)  . To ensure that CPT does not cause catastrophic forgetting of pretraining knowledge, we evaluate each checkpoint on Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU, Hendrycks et al. (2020)) using the lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024), and observe no substantial degradation  (Table 6)  . We also evaluate performance on the held-out test set of 1000 questions using few-shot examples, since these models are not yet instruction-tuned, and find that performance is largely preserved. Table 6 reports these results. We also evaluate the post-trained checkpoints on the held-out MCQs, sampling at temperature of 0.6, top-p of 0.95, repetition penalty of 1.1, and maximum of 1024 new tokens  (Table 7)  . An increasing trend in scores suggests successful training and that it is less likely that the selected models have been trained on the data from QuALITY (an average improvement of 8.93 points from Epoch 0 to Epoch 2 across models). A.2.2 TRIVIAQA Training details. We start directly from the post-trained checkpoints released by model providers6, prompting each model to reason before producing its final answer (Figure 7). We follow the same GRPO setup used for QuALITY. However, since we start from more verbose reasoning model, we set the maximum generation length to 1024. Correctness of each rollout is judged by substring match against the provided aliases. 6OLMoE-1B-7B is not thinking model, but it is post-trained and can follow instructions to generate answers in the required format.

To detect hallucinations

sections.content: for models trained on QuALITY, we prompt GPT-4.1-mini with the training question, the gold answer, the models reasoning, and the original story/article to identify hallucinated fact (prompt in Figure 10). We then convert this hallucination into an MCQ (prompt in Figure 11). For TriviaQA, there is no reference text. We first prompt GPT-4.1-mini with the question, the models reasoning, and the answer to extract three candidate hallucinations (prompt in Figure 12). We then verify each with web search, using the tool-use interface (web search preview) (prompt in Figure 14). We select one verified false fact at random for question generation and discard those where all three candidates turn out to be correct. We then convert this hallucination into an MCQ (prompt in Figure 15). For the backtracking analysis in 3  (Table 3)  , we repeat this sampling and question-generation procedure separately rather than partitioning the hallucinations used for analysis in Table 1, to ensure that the number of evaluated questions remains roughly comparable across settings. For each rollout we independently extract three backtracked and three nonbacktracked candidate hallucinations (prompt in Figure 13), verify them using the same web-search procedure, and sample one verified false fact from each category for MCQ generation. We adopt two-step procedure for detecting hallucinations on TriviaQA since running web verification directly over long explanations generated by reasoning models is expensive. The complete process costs approximately $10 for each set in QuALITY and approximately $35 for TriviaQA. Selecting rollouts. To construct HalluSet-train, we randomly choose model-generated rollout with the correct final answer (if one exists), and apply the above procedure. We ignore questions for which the model generated no correct rollout. We also ignore questions for which all rollouts were correct, as this does not contribute to gradient updates. HalluSet-heldout serves as control. We take the 1000 held-out test questions from each dataset, split them into 8 disjoint groups of 125, and assign one group to each checkpoint M0, . . . , M7. We sample rollouts from the corresponding checkpoint for each group and identify hallucination exactly the same way. Because these questions are held-out, no checkpoint is trained or rewarded on them. Inference. We evaluate each checkpoint on HalluSet-train and HalluSet-heldout using the same sampling parameters used for the test-set questions in A.2. Frontier LLMs have been widely used for factuality evaluation (Min et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024) and for generating MCQ-style questions (Wang et al., 2024). Following these works, we use frontier LLMs to detect hallucinations (given reference text or web search) and convert them into MCQs, refining all prompts through several rounds of prompt engineering and manual spot-checking, and providing few-shot examples. Frontier LLMs have also been shown to reliably answer questions and verify claims against given document (Shaham et al., 2023; Jacovi et al., 2025) and, with web access, to verify open-domain facts (Wei et al., 2024; 2025) closely matching the settings in which we detect hallucinations. Additionally, one of the authors manually verified 200 randomly sampled TriviaQA facts labeled as hallucinated against the web and found precision of 98%. Similarly, one of the authors also manually verified the backtracking labels for 200 randomly sampled claims from TriviaQA, finding an annotation accuracy of 87% for backtracked claims and 91% for non-backtracked claims. These results provide further evidence that frontier LLMs can reliably perform these largely non-subjective tasks when given clear instructions.

For each claim, return 1 if the fact is true, and 0 if it is false. Base your evaluation on web searches from reliable sources. If fact is partially true, extremely vague, or can not be verified, mark it as true. If it is definitely wrong, mark it as false. Return JSON object with exactly these keys: "f1", "f2", "f3", where each value is 0 or 1. Return nothing else. Figure 14: Prompt for checking hallucinations using web search. We conservatively mark partially true, vague, or unverifiable claims as true to reduce false positives, since our goal is to identify clearly false factual claims as hallucinations.

sections.title: Prompt for generating MCQs from hallucinations for TriviaQA
sections.content: An LLM generated hallucinated fact. hallucinated fact is fact that contradicts world knowledge and truth. Your task is to create multiple-choice question that tests this hallucinated fact, i.e., the correct answer to your generated MCQ should be the hallucinated fact. Hallucinated Fact produced by the LLM: {hallucinated_fact} Instructions: - Create one MCQ question that directly tests the given hallucinated (incorrect) fact. - The correct answer to the question you frame should be the hallucinated fact (or close paraphrase of it). - Add 3 plausible but wrong distractor options. None of the options should be "none of the above" or "all of the above". - Avoid using negations while phrasing any question or any option, i.e., avoid words or constructions such as 'not'. - The question should sound like standalone MCQ question, i.e., it should NOT start with or contain phrases like "According to the LLM's incorrect fact...", "According to the hallucinated detail...", etc. - Return ONLY valid Python dictionary with exactly these keys: testing_question, option1, option2, option3, option4, correct_answer. - correct_answer must be only 1, 2, 3, or 4 (integer), indicating which option is correct. - No explanation, no extra text - just the dictionary. --- FEW-SHOT EXAMPLES --- Figure 15: Prompt for generating MCQs from hallucinations for TriviaQA.

sections.title: Prompt for identifying all hallucinations on QuALITY data
sections.content: You are fact-checking assistant specializing in identifying hallucinated reasoning in LLM outputs. An LLM was given the following question about an article. The LLM first reasoned about the question and then answered it. Its reasoning may contain hallucinated (incorrect) facts not supported by the article. Article: {article} Question: {question} LLM Reasoning: {model_reasoning} LLM Answer: {model_answer} Your task: Split the LLM Reasoning into individual sentences. For each sentence, decide whether it is hallucination (a fact that is NOT supported by the article) or not. Label each sentence with 0 if it is hallucinated, 1 if it is not hallucinated, and 2 if it contains no factual information at all. Return ONLY valid JSON object where each key is sentence from the reasoning (verbatim, as complete sentence) and each value is 0, 1, or 2. Do not add any justifications, explanations, markdown, or other text. Return nothing else. Figure 16: Prompt for identifying hallucinations in reasoning trace sentences using GPT-5.1-mini for QuALITY. We use an identical prompt for TriviaQA, but we do not use web search here, as running it over every sentence of long reasoning trace is expensive.
